concepts.name: Pattern as reusable solution
concepts.summary: Recall that a design pattern is a named, proven solution template to a recurring design problem, not finished code or a library.

concepts.name: Problem, solution, consequences structure
concepts.summary: Explain that a pattern is described by the problem it addresses, the solution's structure and the trade-offs it brings.

concepts.name: Creational, structural, behavioural categories
concepts.summary: Recall the three classic categories and what kind of concern each groups: object creation, composition, and interaction.

concepts.name: Shared pattern vocabulary
concepts.summary: Explain how pattern names let developers communicate design intent concisely.

concepts.name: Coupling and flexibility motivation
concepts.summary: Understand that many patterns exist to reduce coupling between classes so that code is easier to change.

concepts.name: Interfaces and polymorphism in patterns
concepts.summary: Understand that most patterns rely on abstract types and polymorphism so callers depend on interfaces rather than concrete classes.

misconceptions.text: A design pattern is a ready-made piece of code or library you can copy in unchanged.
Using more patterns always makes a design better.
Patterns are specific to one programming language.

concepts.name: Factory Method and simple factory
concepts.summary: Implement a factory that hides which concrete class is created so client code depends only on an interface.

concepts.name: Observer subscription and notification
concepts.summary: Implement a subject that notifies registered observers of state changes without knowing their concrete types.

concepts.name: Singleton and its drawbacks
concepts.summary: Explain how a singleton restricts a class to one instance and why global state makes it hard to test.

concepts.name: Composition over inheritance
concepts.summary: Apply object composition instead of subclassing to vary behaviour flexibly.

concepts.name: Strategy as interchangeable algorithms
concepts.summary: Encapsulate a family of algorithms behind one interface and swap them at runtime via composition.

concepts.name: Decorator wrapping behaviour
concepts.summary: Add responsibilities to an object dynamically by wrapping it in objects that share its interface.

concepts.name: Reading UML class diagrams of patterns
concepts.summary: Interpret a class diagram of a pattern and map its roles to concrete classes.

misconceptions.text: Strategy and inheritance with overridden methods are the same thing.
Singleton is a harmless way to share data across the program.
A decorator must change the interface of the object it wraps.

concepts.name: Abstract Factory and Builder
concepts.summary: Choose between Abstract Factory for related product families and Builder for stepwise construction of complex objects.

concepts.name: Adapter versus Facade versus Proxy
concepts.summary: Distinguish wrapper patterns by intent: converting interfaces, simplifying subsystems, or controlling access.

concepts.name: Command and undo
concepts.summary: Encapsulate requests as objects to support queuing, logging and undoable operations.

concepts.name: State versus Strategy
concepts.summary: Analyse how State changes behaviour with internal transitions while Strategy is chosen externally despite similar structure.

concepts.name: Composite for tree structures
concepts.summary: Treat individual objects and groups uniformly through a shared component interface.

concepts.name: Template Method and hooks
concepts.summary: Define an algorithm skeleton in a base class while subclasses override specific steps.

concepts.name: Matching patterns to design problems
concepts.summary: Identify the force or smell in code, such as large conditionals or tight coupling, and select the pattern that addresses it.

concepts.name: Dependency injection and factories
concepts.summary: Pass dependencies in from outside, and decide when injection replaces a factory or singleton.

misconceptions.text: Adapter, Facade and Proxy are interchangeable because they all wrap another object.
State and Strategy are identical because their class diagrams look the same.
Dependency injection is just another name for the factory pattern.

concepts.name: Evaluating pattern trade-offs
concepts.summary: Judge whether a pattern's added indirection and classes are justified by the actual variation and change expected.

concepts.name: Recognising overengineering
concepts.summary: Detect premature or unnecessary pattern use and decide to keep the simpler design.

concepts.name: Refactoring toward patterns
concepts.summary: Evolve existing code toward a pattern in small safe steps once duplication or rigidity appears.

concepts.name: Combining patterns
concepts.summary: Analyse how patterns cooperate, such as Composite with Visitor or Command with Memento, and where the combination adds complexity.

concepts.name: Patterns and language features
concepts.summary: Evaluate when first-class functions, closures, enums or generics make a classic pattern unnecessary.

concepts.name: Visitor and double dispatch
concepts.summary: Analyse how Visitor adds operations to a stable class hierarchy and the cost when the hierarchy changes.

concepts.name: Patterns and testability
concepts.summary: Assess how patterns affect isolation, mocking and test seams in a design.

misconceptions.text: A good design should apply a pattern wherever one could fit.
Visitor is always the right way to add new operations to a class hierarchy.
Patterns must be implemented exactly as the textbook class diagram shows.

concepts.name: Designing domain-specific patterns
concepts.summary: Distil a recurring problem in a domain into a new documented pattern with context, forces, solution and consequences.

concepts.name: Pattern languages and architecture
concepts.summary: Compose related patterns into a coherent language that guides design decisions across a system.

concepts.name: Critiquing pattern-heavy codebases
concepts.summary: Evaluate an existing codebase for misapplied, missing or accidental patterns and recommend changes.

concepts.name: Patterns across paradigms
concepts.summary: Judge how pattern intents translate to functional, concurrent and distributed contexts and where object-oriented forms fail.

concepts.name: Evolving designs under change
concepts.summary: Create designs that anticipate likely axes of change and decide which flexibility to build now versus defer.

concepts.name: Teaching and governing pattern use
concepts.summary: Establish team conventions, documentation and review practices that foster sound pattern use.

misconceptions.text: Patterns are a complete catalogue, so every design problem already has a named pattern.
Object-oriented patterns apply unchanged in functional and distributed systems.
Building maximum flexibility up front is the safest way to handle future change.
